description: When an unborn child is injured or killed in a car accident, do the parents have a claim? Georgia's "quickening" rule and why the law should be reformed.
shortAnswer: In Georgia, "It depends." In order to recover for injuries to an unborn child, it must be shown that at the time of the injury/death the child had reached a stage in its development where the mother could feel fetal movement. This has been recognized to occur somewhere between the 10th week and 4th month of pregnancy.

faq.q: What does "quickening" mean under Georgia law?
faq.a: An unborn child that has quickened and then is injured or killed has legal rights. An unborn child that has not reached that stage of development has none. The Courts have held that the relevant question is whether the baby has reached the stage where the mother can feel fetal movement.

faq.q: How do you prove quickening in a Georgia unborn child injury claim?
faq.a: The key to proving quickening is to have some documentation (commonly a medical record) that the mother had been feeling fetal movement prior to the injury or the testimony of a doctor that the baby had reached the stage of development where the mother could have felt movement.

faq.q: How does Georgia's rule differ from other states?
faq.a: Georgia is unique in its adherence to the legal fiction of "quickening." The majority of jurisdictions that recognize a cause of action for wrongful death of a fetus limit such actions to claims arising after the fetus is viable. Only a few states recognize a cause of action for wrongful death at any point in a pregnancy.

faq.q: Should Georgia allow claims for an unborn child injured at any stage of pregnancy?
faq.a: I believe Georgia law should recognize a cause of action for wrongful death or injury to an unborn child at any point in a pregnancy when the death or injury flows from the negligence of a person other than a family member.
